zujose

R code that talks to OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect providers, or that issues tokens from a Shiny or Plumber app, has to sign, check and decrypt JSON Web Tokens. Getting that right is mostly about what a library refuses: a token that names its own algorithm, a key smuggled in its header, an expired claim that nobody looked at.

zujose implements the JOSE standards, JWS, JWE, JWK and JWT (RFC 7515 to 7519), in both the compact and the JSON serializations, with the defaults of RFC 8725, the JWT best current practices.

  • You name the algorithms. Every function that checks a token takes an algorithms argument with no default, and the key must agree with it. none does not exist.
  • Claims are checked in the same call. jwt_decode() verifies the signature and then exp, nbf, aud, iss and whatever else you ask for. There is no second step to forget.
  • Keys come only from you. A key a token names for itself, as jwk, jku, x5c or x5u in its header, is never used, and zujose never fetches anything.
  • Every algorithm of RFC 7518 but none: HMAC, RSA, RSA-PSS and ECDSA signatures; AES key wrap, AES-GCM key wrap, PBES2, RSA-OAEP and ECDH-ES (including X25519) key management; AES-CBC-HMAC and AES-GCM content encryption. RSA1_5 is accepted for decryption only.
  • Pure R. zujose has no compiled code. The cryptography comes from zucrypt, so no system library is needed.

Installation

zujose is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub, which also installs the development version of zucrypt it needs:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zujose")

Usage 

library(zujose)

An API that issues its own tokens needs a key. This one is a random 256-bit HMAC key, meant for HS256 only:

key <- jwk_generate("oct", alg = "HS256", kid = "api-2026")
key
#> <jwk> oct, 256 bits
#>   kid "api-2026"
#>   alg HS256
#>   private: yes (not shown)

Sign a set of claims as a JWT that expires in an hour:

jwt <- jwt_encode(
  list(sub = "user-17", aud = "orders-api"),
  key,
  expires_in = 3600
)
jwt
#> [1] "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImFwaS0yMDI2IiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyLTE3IiwiYXVkIjoib3JkZXJzLWFwaSIsImV4cCI6MTc5MzcyMjM2MiwiaWF0IjoxNzkzNzE4NzYyfQ.PMjRsBHiZRKEaay3BqEdThCQnP-6c34Xoud6ZnfaVcA"

To check it, name the algorithm and the audience you accept. The result is the claims, with the times as POSIXct:

claims <- jwt_decode(jwt, key, algorithms = "HS256", audience = "orders-api")
claims$sub
#> [1] "user-17"
claims$exp
#> [1] "2026-11-03 16:12:42 UTC"

A token meant for another service is refused:

jwt_decode(jwt, key, algorithms = "HS256", audience = "billing-api")
#> Error in `jwt_decode()`:
#> ! The token is not for this `audience`.

Each failure has a class of its own, so code can catch one cause without reading the message:

tryCatch(
  jwt_decode(jwt, key, algorithms = "HS256", audience = "billing-api"),
  zujose_audience_error = function(e) "403: wrong audience"
)
#> [1] "403: wrong audience"

Encryption takes a key of its own, because a key fits only the algorithms it is for. This one wraps the content key of a JWE with AES key wrap, and the content is encrypted with AES-GCM:

kek <- jwk_generate("oct", alg = "A256KW")
jwe <- jwe_encrypt("account 42: balance 100", kek, enc = "A256GCM")
rawToChar(jwe_decrypt(jwe, kek, "A256KW", "A256GCM")$plaintext)
#> [1] "account 42: balance 100"

Each function is named after the object it works on, jwt_*, jws_*, jwe_* or jwk_*; the token or payload comes first and the key second; and a token is only ever read without being checked by jose_peek(), whose result says so when printed.

Related work

zujose is checked against the RFC 7520 cookbook and the vectors of RFCs 7515 to 7518, 7638, 7797 and 8037. Its JWS and JWT code is checked against tokens made by PyJWT, and its JWE code against jwcrypto in both directions. The CRAN package jose covers JWK, JWS and JWT on top of OpenSSL.
